item.title: Trump’s Ballroom Is Rising at Breakneck Speed: 20 Hours a Day, 7 Days a Week
item.description:
With the fate of his ballroom tied up in court, President Trump is racing against the clock.

He has enlisted a team of 250 workers to push ahead with construction 20 hours a day, seven days a week to complete as much work as quickly as possible. This week, there are plans to install one million pounds of rebar and pour 3,000 cubic yards of concrete for a project that is now two-thirds complete, the administration said in a court filing.

Now, with the matter pending before the Supreme Court, the Trump administration is making a practical appeal to the justices: The ballroom is simply too far along to be stopped now.

“His strategy clearly is to change the reality on the ground so that instead of preserving the status quo, those who rightly invoke the law against what he’s doing are put in a position of having to undo something that is already a fait accompli,” said Laurence H. Tribe, an emeritus university professor of constitutional law at Harvard.

For years, Mr. Trump has argued that the White House should have its own ballroom, saying it was a matter of prestige on the world stage. A ballroom, he said, would allow officials to hold big events for special guests without needing to erect a tent on the South Lawn.

In recent months, as preservationists and other critics have tried to halt or at least slow down the project, Mr. Trump has offered a new justification: national security. Essentially, Mr. Trump is treating the ballroom and the military bunker underneath it as one and the same.

The bunker — officially known as the Presidential Emergency Operations Center, or PEOC — was built during World War II beneath what was once the East Wing, which Mr. Trump tore down last year to make way for his ballroom.

Now, he speaks about the two projects in the same breath.

After an armed man rushed the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in April, for example, Mr. Trump said on social media that the mayhem had proved the need for “the Militarily Top Secret Ballroom currently under construction at the White House.”

Mr. Trump demolished the East Wing last October without seeking any approvals or submitting construction or demolition plans to Congress. While he did bring the project before two review panels whose leaders he had appointed, Mr. Trump has continued to change the plans from the designs they authorized.

Several federal court rulings have found that the president exceeded his authority by moving ahead without congressional approval, but the decisions have been paused pending appeals — which means the construction can go on at least until Friday, when an appeals court order to halt the aboveground construction goes into effect.

The case is also pending before the Supreme Court.

Last week, the Trump administration told the Supreme Court the president was adding flashy golden seals on the outside of the ballroom, a design element that was never submitted to the Commission of Fine Arts.

Joshua Fisher, the director of White House management and administration, told the court that a concrete-and-steel superstructure had already been built that stretches five stories deep and 70 feet high.

Mr. Fisher said 80 percent of the rebar for the project had been placed, and the concrete poured.

He said $335 million of the $400 million needed for the project had been raised from private donors. He estimated the construction was 65 percent complete.

Mr. Fisher said that the ballroom’s columns were being carved by renowned Italian artists, and that the building would be sturdy enough to withstand a nuclear blast.

“Given the current progress, the superstructure is beyond the point of return,” Mr. Fisher wrote. He added that even if the Supreme Court ordered the plans for the building altered or the building taken down, “there would be no way to do so.”

The message was clear: The ballroom cannot be undone.

But in a filing on Tuesday, the preservationists challenging the project told the justices that the administration was trying to “outrun judicial review” by suggesting that it was too late to stop the construction.

“They tell this court that because the ballroom is being built with the type of concrete used ‘in nuclear power plants,’ it will soon be ‘virtually impossible to deconstruct,’” according to the filing.

Lawyers for the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard America’s historic buildings, said the administration had intentionally accelerated construction “in an effort to put their illegal ballroom” beyond judicial intervention.

They have pointed to the Constitution and several federal laws that state Congress must approve such a project. One federal law says, “A building or structure shall not be erected on any reservation, park or public grounds of the federal government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”

Lower court judges have sided with the preservationists, ruling that Congress must first sign off on the expansion and renovation of the White House complex.

“Efforts to foil judicial review and arrogate Congress’s exclusive powers should not be rewarded with a stay that allows petitioners to complete a ballroom they lacked any authority to commence in the first place,” said the trust’s lawyers, led by Thaddeus A. Heuer.

In its filing on Tuesday, the trust suggested that the Supreme Court temporarily halt the aboveground work and then quickly schedule oral arguments for October or November to formally decide whether the project can proceed. If the justices do not press pause now, the trust said, the project is on track to be substantially finished this fall and it will be too late.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, has argued that the ballroom is inextricably linked to the broader national security needs of the White House complex. He said the structure is built with hardened concrete, steel and rebar; protective missile-resistant columns, roofs and beams; droneproof ceilings and roofs; and bullet-, ballistic- and blastproof glass. It includes bomb shelters, state-of-the-art hospital and medical facilities, protective partitioning between all areas of the building, top secret military structures and equipment, military-grade venting, a single integrated air conditioning and heating system, sniper nests and a drone port on top.

Mr. Sauer has also pushed back on the assertion in the unfavorable appeals court ruling that Mr. Trump is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House. “The president of the United States of America is not a tenant, but rather the sole, elected head of the executive branch,” he wrote, adding that other presidents had taken steps to renovate the White House.

The Supreme Court’s conservative majority has often been receptive to the Trump administration’s efforts to expand presidential power, but it has also ruled against some of Mr. Trump’s signature initiatives. The justices are expected to issue an order before the appeals court ruling that would halt construction takes effect on Friday.

Kimberly Wehle, a law professor at the University of Baltimore, said that Mr. Trump had been pushing to expand the powers of the presidency for years, and that attempting to construct a massive new building on White House grounds without lawmakers’ approval is his latest step.

“It’s so symbolic that he literally bulldozes the White House and says, ‘What are you going to do about it?’” she said. “They’re making this general generic argument that ‘I’m the president, so it’s national security, I can do whatever I want.’ That is a very steep, slippery slope into unlimited power in the presidency.”

item.title: Penn State Fraternity Members Are Charged in Cocaine Trafficking Case
item.description:
Pennsylvania’s attorney general on Monday charged 13 former and current Penn State students with felonies and misdemeanors related to a cocaine trafficking operation that he said involved packaging the drug at fraternity houses and distributing it to students.

Six of the defendants are current students, Wyatt DuBois, a spokesman for Penn State, said Tuesday morning.

Four defendants face charges of felony corrupt organizations and conspiracy, among other offenses, while a fifth is charged with felony conspiracy and other crimes. Eight others were charged with misdemeanor offenses, like possession, according to the grand jury indictment.

A 14th person, the father of a student, was charged with tampering with evidence and hindering the investigation.

Two of the defendants, Agostino Abbatiello and Thomas Robinson, were the main suppliers of the drugs, according to Dave Sunday, the attorney general.

Philip Masorti, who is listed as Mr. Abbatiello’s lawyer on court documents, did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. It was unclear whether Mr. Robinson or his father had legal representation.

Making regular trips to Philadelphia and New York to acquire drugs, Mr. Sunday said at a news conference on Monday that they brought back “large amounts of cocaine” to State College, Pa., in 2023 and 2024.

The cocaine was then packaged mainly at the Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon fraternity houses near the Penn State University campus and distributed primarily to students attending the university, the district attorney said.

“This was an upper-level trafficking organization for this region in Pennsylvania,” Mr. Sunday said on Monday.

Members of the Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon fraternity houses helped package the cocaine, he added, sometimes as part of the initiation process for new members. The investigation, which is continuing, did not find drugs being packaged on campus, Mr. Sunday said. He did not say on Monday whether hazing charges would be added.

“The actual drug dealing was largely from friend to friend, fraternity brother to fraternity brother, acquaintance to acquaintance, and at fraternity houses and or during parties or social engagements,” Mr. Sunday said at the news conference.

The defendants facing felony charges were arraigned on Monday morning. Mr. Abbatiello, who failed to appear for his arraignment on Monday, surrendered Tuesday morning and was denied bail.

Penn State administrators suspended the university’s chapter of Delta Upsilon on Monday as they began an investigation. Mr. DuBois said the university “has no authority to sanction” Sigma Chi, because it operates without official approval or recognition from Penn State. But the university still holds individual students there accountable for misconduct, he said.

The executive director of the Delta Upsilon International Fraternity, Justin Kirk, said in a statement that “the individuals associated with Delta Upsilon have either been expelled, suspended or resigned” from the fraternity.

Sigma Chi’s executive director, Michael Church, said that the three members of its fraternity charged in the case had been suspended, as had the Penn State chapter. He said that the organization would investigate whether the allegations involved just individual conduct, or organized chapter activity.

“This conduct is an egregious violation of our values and has no place in our fraternity, community, or society,” Mr. Church said on Tuesday.

“We are horrified by these serious allegations against current and former students,” Andrea Dowhower, Penn State’s vice president for student affairs, said in a statement on Monday. She added, “We will cooperate with law enforcement in any way we can.”

Law enforcement officers tracked the men and learned how the cocaine was obtained, packaged and sold as early as January 2023, according to the grand jury indictment.

Beginning in September 2024, law enforcement officers used a confidential informant to buy cocaine from a source linked to the two fraternity houses, according to the grand jury indictment.

“What we wanted to do is make sure that we took the time to arrest all of these individuals,” Mr. Sunday said at the news conference, “so that we could do our best to root out this criminal organization to stop it from being able to continue to deal cocaine in the future.”

Mr. Sunday said that Thomas Robinson’s father, Paul Robinson, “took steps to conceal evidence, including a safe containing drugs and cash, and obstruct this investigation.”

item.title: University of Michigan Names President After Prior Pick Faced Brain Cancer
item.description:
The University of Michigan has picked Vanderbilt University’s top academic officer to become its new leader, months after its last selection could not take the job because of a brain cancer diagnosis.

The university’s board announced on Tuesday that it had selected C. Cybele Raver, a psychology professor who serves as Vanderbilt’s provost, as its next president. Pending a formal board vote in September, Dr. Raver is set to begin in December.

Dr. Raver will take the helm of Michigan, the 53,000-student public university with more than $2 billion in annual research, at a moment when the value of higher education is being questioned by the federal government and state legislatures.

In a statement, Dr. Raver spoke of “this pivotal moment in higher education.”

“Michigan’s scale and impact across research, education, economic growth and public service are unmatched, and I’m eager to build on its remarkable legacy,” Dr. Raver said.

Dr. Raver’s research on children’s development and other topics at Vanderbilt has attracted more than $24 million from funding agencies, Michigan officials said. Dr. Raver, who holds a doctorate in developmental psychology from Yale University, has previously served as deputy provost at New York University.

Her boss at Vanderbilt, Daniel Diermeier, the chancellor, said in a statement that, under her leadership, the university started the College of Connected Computing, exceeded $1 billion in annual research and expanded the university’s footprint in places like New York and San Francisco.

“Cybele’s impact on Vanderbilt has been profound,” he said.

Vanderbilt University has been vocal in arguing that higher education should pay more attention to viewpoint diversity and take other steps to regain public trust. The university, along with Washington University in St. Louis, recently commissioned a report that found that scholarship in the humanities and social sciences had become too political.

The report has been controversial among some faculty members. Derek Peterson, who recently stepped down as chair of the University of Michigan’s faculty senate, said Dr. Raver’s scholarship was “impressive.”

But he voiced concerns about the Vanderbilt report.

“This is a place where many of us (myself included) practice scholarship in the service of social justice,” he said in an email, adding that the Vanderbilt report “gives up a very great amount of ground to Trump’s agenda for higher education.”

Dr. Peterson acknowledged he did not know Dr. Raver’s views on the report. Dr. Raver could not be reached for this story.

The University of Michigan has been searching for a leader since May 2025, when Santa Ono left to lead the University of Florida. Dr. Ono’s candidacy was ultimately rejected by the Florida system’s board, which said the longtime college president had supported diversity measures and been too lenient on pro-Palestinian student activists.

The university in January appointed Kent D. Syverud, Syracuse University’s chancellor, to the lead the school. Mr. Syverud announced in April that he had been diagnosed with brain cancer. He instead joined Michigan as a law professor and adviser to the board.

item.title: Trump Officials Ignored Their Own University Investigators, Lawyer Says
item.description:
Trump administration officials ignored the recommendations of their own investigators as they pushed to find civil rights violations at three Ivy League universities, according to a whistle-blower complaint released Tuesday.

The Aug. 17 account came from a former Department of Justice civil rights lawyer, Haley Van Erem, and colleagues whose names were redacted, who said they were assigned in 2025 to an administration task force on antisemitism. Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee released the account on Tuesday.

In the complaint, the lawyers accuse administration officials of using campus antisemitism as a pretext to cut federal grants to pressure Brown, Columbia and Harvard. Trump officials had “a predetermined, outcome‑driven approach to enforcement rather than a fact‑based investigative process,” it said, while investigators said they did not have the evidence to conclude the schools had broken the law.

Under pressure from the government, two of the schools, Brown and Columbia, agreed to settlements with the administration. Harvard has so far prevailed in a series of court fights against the government and has not reached a settlement with the government.

The complaint says that when Ms. Van Erem and others “raised issues with the lack of a factual basis” to establish that the schools had broken the law, “their disagreements were sidelined or they faced reprimands.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Health and Human Services and the Justice Department.

Ms. Van Erem had been temporarily assigned to the health department, which oversees some of the largest research funding streams to universities, during the period described in her account. The department did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Tuesday.

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said by email: “While at the D.O.J., Ms. Haley Van Erem did not work on university investigations. And for all matters, the department stands behind the integrity of these investigations.”

In the case of Brown, investigators, including Ms. Van Erem, were told in April 2025 of a plan to “systematically interview Middle East studies professors, particularly Muslim faculty” to see if they would say anything that could be labeled antisemitic, the document states.

Later that month, the lawyers concluded that the investigation into Brown did not find a violation of Title VI, which prohibits discrimination by institutions that receive federal money.

Ms. Van Erem suggested sending Brown a “closure letter reflecting the team’s conclusion that there were no Title VI violations at Brown, noting such action might restore credibility to the investigations,” the complaint states. But Daniel Shieh, a top official in the health department’s civil rights office, said that administration “higher ups” would not accept closing the investigation because “everything is sequenced,” according to Ms. Van Erem’s account.

Ms. Van Erem took that to mean that the investigations were being coordinated based on politics, not the law, the complaint says.

Mr. Shieh did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last July, as part of a settlement with the government, Brown agreed to put $50 million toward work force development. It also agreed to a set of policies that more closely aligned the university with the Trump administration’s ideology, including around gender, and to a three-year arrangement for the government to monitor its compliance.

A spokesman for Brown, Brian Clark, said by email that the university had not been told it had violated the law.

“Even so,” he said, “a freeze on funding for the university’s federally sponsored medical and health sciences research had posed enormous challenges for Brown’s research mission and financial sustainability.”

Also in April 2025, according to the complaint, Sean Keveney, who was then the health department’s acting general counsel, told Ms. Van Erem that the White House had ordered the department to pull grants from Harvard. He showed her proposed settlement terms for Harvard, which included “installing a provost to oversee curriculum, ending D.E.I. programs, placing endowment money in trusts the government could seize and investing in programs in Israel,” the complaint states.

Mr. Keveney later sent demands to Harvard, whose leaders found them so over the top that the university decided to sue. People familiar with the episode later claimed the demands were sent by mistake. The university did not comment on Tuesday.

Democrats were quick to assail the administration over Ms. Van Erem’s account. Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the House Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, called the administration’s antisemitism actions “a prebaked frame-up operation.”

In a 2025 ruling for Harvard, a federal judge in Boston, Allison D. Burroughs, came to a similar conclusion, writing that the administration’s focus on antisemitism at the university was at best “arbitrary and, at worst, pretextual.”

After Judge Burroughs ruled in favor of Harvard in the university’s bid to restore grants — a case that is now before a federal appeals court — the Trump administration this year filed an antisemitism lawsuit against the university. Another federal judge in Boston dismissed that suit this month.

Ms. Van Erem’s accusations align closely with the accounts of others familiar with the Trump administration’s internal debates about universities last year. The New York Times reported this year that early in Mr. Trump’s second term, for example, the Justice Department created a group to investigate the University of California system.

The group was given a month to develop enough evidence to bring accusations of workplace discrimination inside the 10-campus system. One lawyer involved in the matter last year, Ejaz Baluch Jr., told The Times that the group was “only told to investigate cases that were in blue states, and cases or investigations involving red states or that didn’t involve perceived political enemies of the administration never moved forward.”

Federal officials have offered an array of explanations for their pressure campaigns against schools. In some instances, they have argued that the government had the authority to set priorities — and that funneling money to schools that they insisted were hubs of antisemitism was not one of them.

At other moments, they contended that the administration wanted federal research money to be spread through higher education more equally, not directed to the country’s wealthiest schools. And Mr. Trump himself has sometimes been eager to joust with universities, directly steering the terms of engagement between his administration and a handful of universities.

Most notably, Mr. Trump personally had a hand in devising the financial terms in settlement proposals to Columbia, Harvard and the University of California, Los Angeles. (Among those, only Columbia reached a settlement. The university declined to comment on Tuesday.)

Other parts of the federal government have also acknowledged political considerations in their moves against academic researchers. The Energy Department acknowledged in a court filing last month, for instance, that it had moved to end some grants “solely” because the recipients were in states that had voted for Kamala Harris in 2024.

item.title: Liberia Agrees to Take 1,200 Deportees From U.S.
item.description:
The Liberian government said on Tuesday that it would take up to 1,200 deportees from the United States in the next year, one of the largest known deals that the Trump administration has struck to send migrants to countries where they often have no ties.

The first group of 20 deportees is expected to arrive in Liberia on Thursday, the country’s government said in a statement.

The announcement comes as the Trump administration has said it wants to send to Liberia the Salvadoran immigrant Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully expelled last year from his adopted home in Maryland and has since been returned to the United States. His lawyers are currently fighting that effort in the courts.

As part of its push to accelerate deportations, the administration has tried to strike agreements with countries around the world to accept migrants who legally cannot be deported to their own home countries for a variety of reasons, including that some could face persecution there.

In order to convince nations to enter into those agreements, the administration has offered a range of incentives, including paying for foreign security forces and offering to ease visa restrictions or tariffs, as The New York Times has reported.

The Liberian government said on Tuesday that its agreement with the United States was “not a transaction with a quid pro quo.”

“Liberia has not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward in exchange for its consent to participate in the program,” the government said in its statement. “Liberia will receive support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A State Department official said in a statement that the department does not comment on the details of private diplomatic communications with other governments.

The administration has struck third-country deportation deals with more than 30 nations since the start of President Trump’s second term, according to Human Rights First, a nonprofit group that tracks deportations. Those countries include the Dominican Republic, Eswatini, Cameroon and South Sudan.

Such arrangements have come under intense criticism from human rights groups, which say that the Trump administration is dispatching vulnerable migrants to unfamiliar countries, including those with a history of human rights abuses. Some of the deportees have also been subject to detention after being sent to third countries.

The Liberian government said on Tuesday that it would be welcoming the migrants from the United States as “guests” and that they would be offered “the necessary support” to be safe during their stay. They will be free to leave the country or remain and apply for asylum, the government said.

The administration has been pushing to send to Liberia Mr. Abrego Garcia, who spent months in a notorious prison built for terrorists after being deported to El Salvador.

Mr. Abrego Garcia was ultimately brought back to the United States to face human smuggling charges that were later thrown out by a federal judge in Nashville for being an abuse of prosecutorial powers.

Even before the criminal case was dismissed, his lawyers have been fighting his expulsion to Liberia, just as they fought his removal to a series of other African nations, saying that the government cannot simply deport to him to a third country, especially when he has agreed to be sent to Costa Rica and that country’s government has agreed to take him.

item.title: Former Mother-in-Law Describes Lindsay Clancy’s Mental Health Struggle
item.description:
A Massachusetts mother standing trial for murder was “begging for help” in the months before she strangled her three children in the basement, her former mother-in-law testified on Tuesday.

“We were all concerned,” Susan Clancy said when called to the stand by defense lawyers for Lindsay Clancy, 36, who does not deny killing Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, in January 2023. She has pleaded not guilty, citing postpartum psychosis.

Susan Clancy said Lindsay had reached out to her in November 2022, saying that she had been struggling with anxiety, depression and insomnia. At the time, Lindsay had been prescribed anti-depressants that made her feel worse, Susan said.

The high-profile trial began three weeks ago, with prosecutors arguing that Lindsay Clancy had carefully planned the killings, plotting to get her husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the house before she choked their children with an exercise band. The prosecution rested on Monday after more than 70 witnesses.

The defense started on Monday by calling people to the stand who could paint Lindsay Clancy as a warm mother. Her former mother-in-law, whose son divorced Ms. Clancy after the killings, described the defendant as “very nurturing, very loving.”

In text messages with her mother-in-law in the months leading up to the children’s deaths, Ms. Clancy expressed concern that she had developed a dependency on benzodiazepines, powerful psychiatric drugs that can cause an overdose if misused.

“We are just throwing different meds in the mix that are not addressing the real issue,” Lindsay Clancy wrote on Nov. 29. The following day, she texted her mother-in-law: “I’m not OK, and I’m terrified of taking meds tonight.”

Susan Clancy said she worked for nearly four decades as a labor and delivery nurse. She testified that she had reached out to her colleagues who ran a clinic for women struggling with postpartum depression in hopes that they could help Lindsay, and connected her to a nurse practitioner who ran the clinic.

Several medical professionals testified on Tuesday about indications that Ms. Clancy had displayed symptoms consistent with postpartum depression in the months before the killings.

Dr. Donald Condie, a forensic psychiatrist who did not treat Ms. Clancy but reviewed her medical records, said a diagnosis of bipolar disorder was also “a very serious possibility.” He listed several medications that different providers had prescribed starting in September, when Ms. Clancy sought psychiatric help.

After that, he said, she called a suicide hotline twice. “In October, she felt that she was numb,” Dr. Condie said. “She talked about not being herself, being worse not better.”

After the killings, Ms. Clancy cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window, in what her lawyers have called a suicide attempt. She experienced traumatic back injuries and is paralyzed.

Dr. Paul Ziesel, a forensic psychologist, testified that he had visits with Ms. Clancy more than 60 times after the killings, starting in February 2023, to document her mental health and determine whether she was fit to stand trial.

Ms. Clancy said during one of those visits that she had “heard a male voice telling her that she didn’t have any choice but she had to kill her children, and then kill herself,” Dr. Ziesel said.

During cross-examination, prosecutors tried to cast doubt on whether Ms. Clancy had truly experienced auditory hallucinations. Dr. Condie, who reviewed her case, acknowledged that there was no record of her telling health care providers about hearing voices until after the children’s deaths.

But he said records indicated that she was scared her children would be taken away by the state if she displayed severe symptoms, and he speculated that fear might have led her to withhold some of what she was experiencing from doctors.

The defense will continue calling witnesses on Wednesday. If Ms. Clancy is found guilty, she faces life in prison without the possibility of parole. If she is found not guilty, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital.

item.title: When to Expect Results in Alaska, California, Florida and Wyoming
item.description:
Voters in Alaska, Florida and Wyoming head to the polls today to vote in their states’ primaries, and voters in California’s 14th Congressional District will vote in a special general election.

Here’s when to expect results.

Polls in Florida will close at 7 p.m. local time; most of the state observes Eastern time, except for the western Panhandle, which is on Central time. Polls there will close at 8 p.m. Eastern.

Results will likely be in late on Tuesday, officials say, based on how quickly votes were counted and reported in the state’s last primary. Readers can follow along here with The New York Times’s vote tracker.

Results will be certified when the state’s election canvassing commission convenes, on Sept. 1.

In Wyoming, polls will close at 7 p.m. local time (9 p.m. Eastern), at which point counties will begin tabulating early votes and those that came in on Election Day. Election officials anticipate that most results will be known late on Tuesday night.

You can watch the results come in on Tuesday night with The Times’s vote tracker. The state canvassing board will meet on Sept. 1 to certify the tallies.

California is holding a special general election to fill former Representative Eric Swalwell’s vacated House seat.

Polls will close at 8 p.m. local time (11 p.m. Eastern), at which point the state’s election officials will begin tallying the votes they received through early voting and mail ballots. Election officials say that unofficial results will likely be known late on Tuesday night. The secretary of state will certify the results by Sept. 25.

Follow along with The Times’s vote tracker.

Polls in Alaska close at 8 p.m. local time (12 a.m. Eastern time for most of the state, and 1 a.m. Eastern in the Aleutian Islands, which are an hour behind).

The state is holding what it calls a “pick-one” primary election. Voters will cast their ballots for only one candidate per race, with the four candidates who receive the most top votes in each race advancing to the general election in November.

Alaska’s voting system is organized by regions rather than counties. Election officials anticipate that regions will begin posting results between 8:45 p.m. and 9 p.m. local time on Tuesday, but the timing will vary.

Note, too, that Alaska allows absentee ballots that were postmarked on or before Election Day to be received 10 days after Election Day. It’s possible that race calls will not be made until early Wednesday or later, officials say.

Readers can follow these results on The Times’s vote tracker. The state review board will certify the vote by Aug. 31.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Florida Senate Candidate Alex Vindman
item.description:
Alex Vindman, a former national security official who was a top witness in President Trump’s first impeachment trial, is the front-runner in the Democratic Senate primary in Florida.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Vindman, 51, a first-time candidate.

1. He became nationally known when he testified before Congress in 2019. Mr. Vindman testified about a call between Mr. Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, saying that Mr. Trump pressured Mr. Zelensky to investigate his rivals, including the Biden family. Mr. Vindman was on the call as a National Security Council aide. Mr. Trump, who was acquitted by the Senate, fired Mr. Vindman in 2020. Mr. Vindman later sued, accusing Trump officials of retaliation and intimidation.

2. He has campaigned as a defender of democracy. Mr. Vindman, who moved to Florida in 2023, has introduced himself to voters as someone who has stood up to Mr. Trump. He has also noted that he is a retired Army lieutenant colonel whose family fled communism in Ukraine.

3. He emerged as a serious fund-raiser as soon as he entered the race. Mr. Vindman out-raised his main opponent in the Democratic primary, State Representative Angie Nixon, and the Republican incumbent, Senator Ashley Moody, in the first half of this year. However, Mr. Vindman has also had to spend heavily to grow his donor base, leaving Ms. Moody with more cash on hand.

4. He remains a long shot in a state that leans Republican. Gone are the days in which Florida was the nation’s largest battleground: Mr. Trump won the state by 13 percentage points in 2024. The expense of campaigning in such a large state has been prohibitive for Democrats in recent years.

5. His identical twin brother, Eugene, is already in Congress. Eugene Vindman won a competitive congressional race in Northern Virginia in 2024. He, too, had been removed by Mr. Trump from his role as a lawyer for the National Security Council after the first impeachment trial. As a candidate, Eugene Vindman became a favorite of grass-roots Democratic donors.

Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Florida Senate Candidate Angie Nixon
item.description:
State Representative Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist and union organizer, won a major upset on Tuesday in the Democratic Senate primary in Florida.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Nixon, 42, of Jacksonville, who defeated Alex Vindman, a top witness in President Trump’s first impeachment trial who vastly out-raised her. Ms. Nixon will now face Senator Ashley Moody, a Republican, in conservative-leaning Florida.

1. She is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. Ms. Nixon joined D.S.A. this year, but has downplayed her affiliation with the group, saying it is not central to her political identity. “I’m also a Democrat; I’m also a member of the Florida Public Services Union,” she said in an interview on Tuesday afternoon. The D.S.A. has notched a series of recent victories in House primaries. In the Florida primary, Ms. Nixon was also supported by some progressive House members, including Representatives Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan and Maxwell Frost of Florida. But she was not endorsed by two of the most prominent progressives in Congress, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.

2. She unseated a Democratic state lawmaker in 2020. Ms. Nixon defeated the incumbent, Kimberly Daniels, who had served two terms in the Legislature. Ms. Nixon’s campaign focused on constituent services. “I was running on being the people’s pick — the people’s champion,” she said in the interview, adding that she was heavily outspent in that race and was pregnant during the campaign. “My core campaign promise was that the constituents and Floridians would have the opportunity to reach me and talk to me.” This year, her platform calls for universal health care, higher taxes on the wealthy, abolishing for-profit prisons and raising the federal minimum wage to $25 per hour. “I believe hard-working, everyday people should really get to shape what our economies look like,” Ms. Nixon said in the interview. “Right now, Washington, D.C., is so out of touch.”

At times, the family would stay with her grandmother. “It was stressful,” Ms. Nixon said. “It was riddled with domestic violence.” But she said her mother taught her the value of hard work.

5. She joined a rally that angered some Democrats last weekend. Ms. Nixon was one of a group of progressive candidates at a South Florida rally headlined by Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, an outspoken critic of Israel. Some Florida Democrats objected to Ms. Tlaib’s presence, and organizers moved the event after the host venue backed out. Ms. Nixon said the event was intended to “invigorate and energize young people to get out to vote.”

item.title: Threatening Friends and Courting Enemies in Trump’s ‘Upside-Down World’
item.description:
Once again, President Trump is threatening his country’s own partners with everything from tariffs to bombs. Once again, he is fawning over a nuclear-armed tyrant deemed to be one of the biggest dangers to U.S. security. And once again, the world is left trying to make sense of a United States that has upended the world order that it established eight decades ago.

Nearly 10 years after Mr. Trump first came to the White House on the slogan of America First, his attack-thy-friends, befriend-thy-enemies approach to international relations has become the feature, not the bug, of U.S. foreign policy. Traditional alliances from Europe to Asia to the Middle East have frayed while the president courts those once seen as its adversaries.

Even so, the past few days have thrown the Trumpian worldview into stark relief. Mr. Trump declared that he would bomb Oman, a key friend in the complicated diplomacy of the Middle East, if he decides it is getting in the way of his war with Iran. He was set to impose punitive new tariffs on Canada, once considered the United States’ closest friend. And he announced that he would pull back military support from South Korea, the bulwark of the U.S. network of partners in the Asia-Pacific.

At the same time, he again began sending public mash notes to North Korea’s absolute dictator, Kim Jong-un, with whom by his own description he “fell in love” in his first term. Mr. Kim, who rules one of the most oppressive nations in the world, never did give up his nuclear weapons, as Mr. Trump once declared he would. Instead, Mr. Kim has vastly expanded his nuclear arsenal in defiance of Mr. Trump, who nonetheless remains a suitor, no matter how unrequited.

“He dumps on our friends and cozies up to our enemies,” said James J. Blanchard, a former ambassador to Canada and Democratic governor of Michigan. “If someone once told me that Russia is our friend and Canada is our enemy, I’d have told you we’re in an upside-down world.”

Richard Fontaine, the chief executive of the Center for a New American Security and a former adviser to Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona, said that none of the bombastic threats were new. But he pointed out that Mr. Trump had not always followed through on them. The United States, he noted, had not pulled out of NATO, abandoned South Korea, bombed Oman or seized Canada and Greenland.

“Increasingly, the bullying rhetoric is being priced in by countries around the world,” Mr. Fontaine said. “They don’t dismiss it, but they don’t take the threats literally either. As more and more unfulfilled threats are issued, people listen less. It undermines the president’s credibility.”

Mr. Trump has long argued that his approach to other countries, however unorthodox, makes sense for the United States. Under previous presidents, allies took advantage of America’s security presence and trade rules without reciprocating, Mr. Trump maintains. He sees relatively high trade deficits and relatively low NATO military spending as proof that so-called friends are exploiting the United States.

As for sweet talking North Korea, China, Russia and other longtime adversaries, Mr. Trump contends that the confrontational policies of the past failed to achieve what they set out to, so better to try more diplomacy. He still hopes to reach a nuclear accord with North Korea, seal a comprehensive trade deal with China and reestablish full ties with Russia by brokering an end to Moscow’s war in Ukraine. He has pushed aides for a meeting this fall with Mr. Kim, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The war with Iran has provided a new scorecard for the allies that deserve support and those that do not. Countries that have declined to facilitate military operations against Tehran or use force to help guarantee passage through the Strait of Hormuz have in his view betrayed the United States, even though he never asked for their opinions before starting the war. After targeting Britain, France, Spain, Italy and others for not doing more to help him against Iran, Mr. Trump has now focused his ire on South Korea.

“We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbor, and you’re not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran?” he said this week after announcing that he would scale back joint exercises with South Korea.

By contrast, he went on, “Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect, and we’ve met on numerous occasions, actually, two primary occasions — spoken and spent time. I understand him. He understands me.”

If so, that distinguishes Mr. Kim from European and Asian allies who still do not understand Mr. Trump, even if they have come to expect his volatile outbursts. Until now, presidents of both parties have valued their relationships with overseas friends. And while there have been plenty of moments of tension over the years, they have worked to keep them from escalating too far.

Now the allies are the ones trying to avoid exacerbating the situation. “They grit their teeth and bear it because in the end they do not want to see irreparable damage done to the alliance over the next two years,” said Victor D. Cha, the president of the Geopolitics and Foreign Policy Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “In short, allies may like and trust the U.S. less today, but they still need the U.S.”

Mr. Cha, who was an Asia adviser to President George W. Bush, said that President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea actually has a good relationship with Mr. Trump and does not want to harm that. “Lee is also as transactional as Trump, so if Trump’s outreach to Kim Jong-un works, that is very much in South Korea’s interests,” Mr. Cha said.

The presence of U.S. forces in South Korea since the 1950s war has long irritated Mr. Trump, who sees it in zero-sum terms. In his first term, he sought to pull troops out and cancel military exercises, judging them wasteful and unnecessarily provocative toward his friend in North Korea. He sought to charge South Korea billions of dollars for U.S. protection, and linked security issues to his complaints about Seoul’s trade policies.

Mr. Trump is not the first president interested in bringing troops home from South Korea so long after the war. President Jimmy Carter promised to scale down U.S. forces there, but gave up amid resistance from Congress and his own administration. Donald H. Rumsfeld, who was Mr. Bush’s defense secretary, surprised the South Koreans by redeploying a brigade to Iraq, and never returned it. Today, about 28,500 U.S. troops are stationed in South Korea, according to the Congressional Research Service.

“There could be a strategic case for restructuring the U.S. military presence on the peninsula,” said Michael J. Green, the chief executive of the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney in Australia, “but none for making them a pawn in a flirtation with the world’s cruelest dictator — particularly at a time when North Koreans are coming back from the Ukraine war battle hardened and backed by a larger missile inventory than they had in 2018.”

Oman, for its part, has for years been an important interlocutor between the United States and Iran, helping to facilitate negotiations when the two sides were open to talks. But Mr. Trump has grown increasingly aggravated that Oman has sought to broker a deal with Iran to control the Strait of Hormuz.

He first threatened to mount an unprovoked war on the sultanate in May, saying that “Oman will behave just like everybody else or we’ll have to blow them up.” On Monday, he lashed out again, declaring that if Oman “gets in the way” of his efforts to reach an agreement with Iran, “we’ll bomb the shit out of them.”

Canada faces a different form of hostility from Mr. Trump, who vowed to slap new tariffs of 50 percent on more than 500 Canadian goods, including hockey sticks and cheese, Tuesday at midnight. Just 90 minutes before his self-imposed deadline, Mr. Trump, as he often has done, pulled back from the brink and suspended the tariffs for three days to give more time for talks.

But even if the two sides eventually reach an accord, there remain many points of friction between the neighbors, exacerbated by Mr. Trump’s oft-expressed ambition to take over Canada and make it “the 51st state.” Just last month, the opening of the new Gordie Howe International Bridge linking Detroit with Windsor, Ontario, was delayed for weeks over various grievances Mr. Trump has with Canada.

Mr. Blanchard said he suspected that the latest eruptions against Canada and other U.S. allies stemmed from Mr. Trump’s inability to bring the Iran war to a close. Neither bombing nor negotiations have forced Iran to surrender control of the Strait of Hormuz or to make verifiable commitments to abandon its nuclear program. The president appears stuck in a geopolitical trap without a clear path forward.

Mr. Fontaine said that Mr. Trump’s approach to allies and adversaries undermined U.S. interests. “There should be benefits to being a friend of America, and costs for being an enemy,” he said, “not the other way around.”

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Senator Ashley Moody of Florida
item.description:
Senator Ashley Moody, who is defending her seat for the first time, won the Republican Senate primary in Florida on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Moody, 51, who is serving her second year in the Senate.

1. She was appointed to the Senate by Gov. Ron DeSantis. Mr. DeSantis, a Republican, named Ms. Moody, a loyal ally, to replace Marco Rubio in the Senate once Mr. Rubio was about to be confirmed as secretary of state. At the time, Ms. Moody was the state’s attorney general, having been elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. Mr. DeSantis praised her “demonstrated record of delivering results.”

2. She is running with President Trump’s endorsement — and without major Republican opposition. Mr. Trump endorsed Ms. Moody in July 2025 and reiterated his support for her again last week, saying that she is “doing a tremendous job.” Ms. Moody’s Senate appointment made her an immediate favorite in the election to finish the remainder of Mr. Rubio’s term, and no well-known Republican candidates challenged her in the primary.

3. She remains little-known to many Florida voters. Despite having won two statewide races, Ms. Moody, polls have shown, has relatively low name recognition for an incumbent, a risk for any politician seeking re-election. But Florida Republicans have huge advantages over Democrats in voter registration, fund-raising and field organizing. And Ms. Moody, her supporters point out, has been underestimated in the past — and won.

4. She is a quieter candidate in a state of big personalities. Some Republicans have worried that Ms. Moody, whom they consider deliberate and effective, is too cautious a campaigner. Her style is much different from those of the gregarious Mr. Rubio and the indefatigable Senator Rick Scott, a fellow Republican. Since Ms. Moody would be assuming a prominent role on the Republican ticket in a year that the party could face mounting losses in the midterm elections, some Republicans hope to see more of her ahead of the November general election.

5. She is a fifth-generation Floridian. Before being elected attorney general, Ms. Moody was a circuit court judge in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, for about a decade. She had earlier worked as a federal prosecutor, and is married to a law enforcement officer.

item.title: Haitians in Springfield Hunker Down as ICE Begins Detentions
item.description:
Federal agents have been detaining small numbers of Haitians over the last week in Springfield, Ohio, according to community leaders and advocates, fueling widespread fear among the immigrants that is prompting many to stay home.

At least 15 Haitians have been detained by federal agents, who have been in the city almost every day since early last week, the local leaders said. More than 100 others have been summoned in recent weeks to Immigration and Customs Enforcement offices miles away, where they have been fitted with electronic ankle monitors that track their movements.

Springfield has been on edge since the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to terminate Temporary Protected Status, a program that shielded 330,000 Haitians nationwide from deportation and granted them legal work authorization.

“People in our community are terrified,” said Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Springfield Haitian Support Center, the local organization that supports Haitians.

“It’s extremely chaotic,” he said. “We have people isolating themselves, refusing to eat.”

The Department of Homeland Security declined to answer questions about enforcement operations in Springfield.

“Every day, D.H.S. is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe,” the department said in a statement. “D.H.S. does not discuss ongoing or future operations.”

ICE has indicated internally that it would push to quickly deport people who recently lost T.P.S., including those from Haiti, Syria, Yemen and South Sudan.

In guidance sent to ICE officers last week and reviewed by The New York Times, the agency said former T.P.S. holders should “first be considered for expedited removal,” a process that allows the government to deport certain immigrants without court proceedings.

The D.H.S. did not respond to a request for comment on the guidance.

In June, a federal appeals court allowed the Trump administration to resume using the fast-track deportation process nationwide. Under previous administrations, expedited removal was used narrowly for undocumented migrants detained near the southern border. But the Trump administration has pushed to expand federal use of this authority.

In Springfield, the support center’s usually crowded waiting room was deserted on Tuesday as word spread that roving unmarked SUVs and a van in a parking lot had been identified as ICE vehicles by volunteers patrolling the streets.

Even as they hunker down, Haitians have been calling the center nonstop seeking answers, said Mr. Dorsainvil. Is it too risky to go to work? How can I get to Canada? What will become of my children if I am arrested?

One of the few people there on Tuesday was Marie, 63, who had an ankle monitor clamped around her leg. A Springfield resident for more than five years, she lost her right to work when T.P.S. ended. She had come to check if it was too late to apply for asylum. (Petitions normally must be filed within one year of entering the country.)

“I am petrified of being deported to Haiti,” she said. “I talked to my family there just yesterday, and they told me they hear gunshots day and night.”

Another visitor, Lucson, 35, supports a wife and two young daughters in Haiti by working at a local auto-parts manufacturer under a work permit tied to his pending asylum application. But he sees the toll around him: Roughly 20 Haitian co-workers were let go when T.P.S. ended, and others have stayed away from work entirely as ICE activity ramped up.

Both immigrants asked to be identified solely by their first names out of fear of retribution from U.S. authorities.

Inside St. Vincent de Paul, a Catholic charity, American volunteers packed food boxes for delivery to Haitian families, many of whom had never needed aid before, said Casey Rollins, the executive director.

“We are taking care of people forced out of their jobs,” said Ms. Rollins, her eye welling with tears.

Haitian residents also require assistance with utilities and rent payments, she said.

Only two families were at the charity, where parents have also been receiving help filling out passport applications for their American-born children and granting power of attorney to trusted friends who could take custody of their children if they are detained.

Springfield, a struggling industrial town for decades, was revitalized by thousands of Haitians who began settling here in recent years after hearing that jobs were plentiful and the cost of living affordable.

The city, home to 10,000 to 15,000 Haitians, was thrust into the contentious immigration debate after President Trump said from the debate stage in September 2024 that the newcomers to the city were eating their neighbors’ pets.

Once in office, his administration moved to strip Temporary Protected Status from Haitians and others. The protection is offered to foreigners already in the United States when conditions are considered too dangerous for safe return to their home countries.

Lower courts ruled that the Trump administration had been motivated by racial animus and had failed to conduct the required assessment of conditions on the ground in Haiti, which has been struggling with political instability, gang violence and food insecurity. But the Supreme Court decided in late June that the administration had the authority to end the program.

Since then, the Trump administration has been under pressure to start rounding up Haitians.

The arrests in Springfield have drawn less attention nationally than the operations in cities like Minneapolis, Chicago and Los Angeles, where federal agents descended in large numbers.

“ICE hasn’t been here on a large scale but their daily raids are scaring people and disrupting the peace of the city,” said Carl Ruby, the pastor of Central Christian Church, founder of a coalition of churches that has organized to protect Haitians.

And the arrests have been random, rather than targeted, he and others said.

Small groups of agents have been detaining immigrants in Springfield as they leave their homes or commute to or from work.

“If they focused on the worst of the worst as they claim, we could support that,” said Mr. Ruby. “Their real goal is to incite fear, hoping that people will go back to Haiti.”

Vulder Marco Dorsainvil, 30, who is a permanent legal resident and Mr. Dorsainvil’s brother, said agents followed him from his apartment complex to a Kroger parking lot, where they boxed in his car between three unmarked vehicles. They released him after he produced a green card.

“They were looking for anybody to take,” he said. “They didn’t know my name.”

Mr. Ruby said that as he watched ICE agents arrest two people on Monday, one of the agents tried to hand him a small figure of Jesus.

“Jesus didn’t want people to hand out meaningless tokens,” Mr. Ruby said. “He wants us to welcome and care for the vulnerable.”

Hamed Aleaziz and Madeleine Ngo contributed reporting.

item.title: Wasserman Schultz Wins Democratic Primary in Historically Black District
item.description:
Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida, whose congressional district was eliminated this year by Republican state lawmakers, won the Democratic primary for the newly redrawn 20th Congressional District on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

Ms. Wasserman Schultz, who is white, defeated Black candidates who had strongly criticized her decision to run in the historically Black district, which includes most of Broward County’s African American and Caribbean American communities.

A spate of Republican gerrymanders across the South this year was almost certain to reduce the number of Black lawmakers in the House. The area that encompasses Florida’s 20th District has long elected a Black representative.

But Ms. Wasserman Schultz, an 11-term incumbent and a former chairwoman of the Democratic National Committee, argued that she had decades of experience representing South Florida at the state and federal levels. Her seniority, she said, would benefit the district’s constituents.

“We have to show the voters and the citizens of this state that the Republicans who cynically tried to rig our map are not going to be rewarded, like they weren’t rewarded today,” Ms. Wasserman Schultz told supporters on Tuesday night in Tamarac, Fla.

Surrounded by her team and some Black community leaders, Ms. Wasserman Schultz wiped away tears and embraced her father, who served as her campaign treasurer for 30 years. During the campaign, Ms. Wasserman Schultz far out-raised her rivals and made a point of attending many community events over the past two months.

Several Black candidates in the race had hoped that Ms. Wasserman Schultz, 59, would choose to run in a different district. But doing so would have required running against a fellow Democratic House member or for a Republican-leaning seat. The 20th District is safely Democratic, so Ms. Wasserman Schultz will be heavily favored to win in the November general election.

In June, four Black Democrats tried to coalesce around a unity candidate to face off against Ms. Wasserman Schultz. But they could not agree on which of them should remain in the contest. (The other three would have had to drop out.)

On Tuesday, Ms. Wasserman Schultz defeated those four candidates: Elijah Manley, a teacher and political activist; former Representative Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick; Dale V.C. Holness, a former Broward County mayor; and Luther Campbell, known as Uncle Luke, from the hip-hop group 2 Live Crew.

Ms. Cherfilus-McCormick resigned from office in April before a scheduled House panel vote to consider expelling her. She has been indicted on criminal charges of embezzling $5 million in federal disaster aid and using it for her campaign. She has denied the accusation and pleaded not guilty.

item.title: Judge Orders New Oversight of Immigrant Children’s Detention
item.description:
A federal judge this week found that officials at immigration detention centers in Texas and California had likely housed children and other detainees at unsafe temperatures and had denied them soap and adequate sleeping conditions.

In an order issued on Monday, Judge Dolly M. Gee of the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles said she was appointing an independent monitor and a special master — an expert assigned to assist her — as she tracks the government’s compliance with a 1997 legal agreement that sets basic standards of care for immigrant children in U.S. custody.

Judge Gee oversees the agreement, known as the Flores settlement, and the plaintiffs have been asking the court to step in, because of what they said was growing evidence that the government was not complying.

Under the Flores settlement, migrants who are 17 years old and younger must be expeditiously released from custody and must receive adequate meals, clean water, clothing, education and medical assistance, among other basic needs.

But the judge found “stark” and “conflicting” differences between the government’s compliance claims and reports from immigrant detainees. In declarations, families said that children were often given only over-the-counter medicine such as Tylenol and ibuprofen in response to a variety of medical concerns.

Families also documented critical delays in care, according to the court filings. A 10-year-old child with a heart murmur had to wait nearly 60 days before seeing a cardiologist. Another child cried out in pain while waiting for treatment for appendicitis. A 2-year-old with diarrhea was sent to a hospital only after six days of fever and repeated visits to a medical center inside a detention facility.

The Trump administration has sought to terminate the Flores settlement, but Judge Gee rejected the first try, in 2019, and last year, she rejected another attempt. The government has appealed her decision and the case is before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

In a response to Judge Gee last month, the government argued against the need for additional oversight, arguing it was in compliance with the Flores settlement and the legal standards for appointing independent monitors had not been met.

But this week, Judge Gee found that the plaintiffs had provided enough evidence to warrant closer oversight.

For at least the next 12 months, Andrea Sheridan Ordin, a former U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, will serve as special master and Paul H. Wise, a Stanford University pediatrician and health policy expert, as independent monitor. The appointees will evaluate conditions at several facilities and will track how long authorities are holding detainees who are 17 or younger.

The court’s new oversight effort covers children held by Customs and Border Protection in its Rio Grande Valley, El Paso and San Diego sectors, and children held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at hotels and in the South Texas Family Residential Center, a detention facility in Dilley, Texas.

At the Dilley facility, they will be looking specifically at whether ICE is providing minors appropriate access to medical care and giving detainees notice of their rights under the legal agreement. The order this week was the culmination of a series of meetings the judge has been holding since July 2025 with the parties in the case to review the plaintiffs’ concerns.

The court found that the government may have kept faulty records that mask how long children have been held, and that the plaintiffs had been able to show persistent safety and sanitary failures at the sectors now under watch.

In the Rio Grande Valley, El Paso and San Diego sectors, families and their children continued to raise complaints of “freezing temperatures” at holding cells that have colloquially become known as “hieleras” — “iceboxes” in Spanish. In the San Diego sector, detainees also submitted declarations saying lights were on day and night.

Although C.B.P. facilities are meant to be only temporary holding places, the average detention times for immigrant minors crossing the border with families exceeded the 72-hour target limit between March and June 2026. Under the settlement, children are supposed to be transferred out of C.B.P. facilities within 72 hours and out of ICE custody within roughly 20 days.

At the family detention center in Dilley, which has held, on average, around 235 children over the past year, the plaintiffs’ lawyers estimated that about 1,560 minors had been detained for longer than 20 days, based on six months of data reported to the court.

Seamus Hughes and Allison McCann contributed reporting.

item.title: Jared Moskowitz, Centrist Democrat From Florida, Beats Back Challenge From Left
item.description:
Jared Moskowitz, a centrist Democrat and one of the most vocal supporters of Israel in the House, won his primary in Florida’s 25th Congressional District on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, despite a high-profile challenge from a democratic socialist.

Mr. Moskowitz, who is seeking a third term, is running in a new district stretching along the Atlantic coastline from Miami-Dade to Palm Beach Counties. Mr. Moskowitz’s former district, largely in blue-leaning Broward County, was eliminated when state Republicans redrew the congressional map to favor them. He will face Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton.

Still, Mr. Moskowitz has an opportunity to preserve a Democratic seat. His race is considered the most competitive in the state. The Cook Political Report rated it as Florida’s only tossup election.

His first test on Tuesday may have been just as significant as his next. Oliver Larkin, a union organizer and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ran an insurgent campaign that captured national attention as another potential opportunity for progressives to win a primary against incumbent Democrats.

Mr. Larkin most likely would have faced an uphill climb in the general election in such a conservative state. Mr. Moskowitz had establishment backing from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, and he raised significantly more money than Mr. Larkin.

The competitive primary highlighted the growing divide in the Democratic Party over Israel. The district is home to a significant number of Jewish voters.

Mr. Moskowitz, one of the most prominent Jewish Democrats in Congress, has called for “unwavering support” of Israel. He has been a staunch supporter of continued U.S. military aid to Israel, even as more than 100 Democrats in the House have voted to end it. His campaigns have garnered support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying organization.

The issue was one factor in Mr. Moskowitz’s decision to decline interviews, or debates with Mr. Larkin, who has described himself as anti-Zionist and called Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide.

“I’m not going to platform him. He’s running against me solely on my religion,” Mr. Moskowitz told WLRN, the Miami public radio station. Mr. Larkin has said he opposes antisemitism.

The congressman has touted “a record of action,” including, as a state lawmaker, shepherding aggressive gun control legislation in the aftermath of the shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018. Mr. Moskowitz attended the school as a teenager.

In 2024, Mr. Moskowitz was the target of an assassination plot. He said at the time that a man taken into custody was found with a manifesto containing antisemitic rhetoric and a target list including the congressman’s name.

Mr. Larkin tried to tie Mr. Moskowitz to Gov. Ron DeSantis, a popular Republican who appointed Mr. Moskowitz to the state’s top emergency management job and the Broward County Commission. Mr. Moskowitz’s campaign emphasized “bipartisan leadership.”

item.title: Sydney Gruters, Wife of R.N.C. Chair, Wins House Primary in Florida With Trump’s Backing
item.description:
Sydney Gruters, a first-time candidate backed by President Trump, handily won her Republican primary in Florida’s sprawling, newly redrawn 16th Congressional District, according to The Associated Press.

Despite having never held office, Ms. Gruters, 44, has been enmeshed in Republican Party politics in Florida. She has spent much of her career working for House members and is married to Joe Gruters, the chairman of the Republican National Committee, who was formerly a state senator and the chairman of the state’s Republican Party.

The couple have received strong endorsements from President Trump. In a July video message, Mr. Trump said Ms. Gruters was “one of the fiercest America First advocates in the country.”

The district Ms. Gruters is vying to represent covers urban, suburban and rural areas near St. Petersburg, encompassing a demographically diverse electorate in a state that has swung to the right in recent years. Tuesday’s primary was the first election that included the district’s new shape. A Republican, Representative Vern Buchanan, has held the seat for the past 20 years; Ms. Gruters formerly worked for him.

During Mr. Trump’s first administration, he appointed Ms. Gruters to be the rural development state director for Florida and the U.S. Virgin Islands in the U.S. Department of Agriculture. She then went on to lead a foundation at the New College of Florida, a public liberal arts college in Sarasota whose politics have shifted rightward under the leadership of Gov. Ron DeSantis.

In that role, she helped oversee the fulfillment of Mr. Trump’s offer to give federal funding to schools that backed his policies on hiring and admissions, including the elimination of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. In exchange, New College received millions of dollars in federal funding.

The new boundaries reflect a statewide redistricting undertaken by Mr. DeSantis this year. The district now includes a largely Black portion of St. Petersburg, the state’s fifth-most populous city, as well as the firmly Republican city of Bradenton and rural areas central to the state’s cattle and citrus industries. It also contains the proposed site of a gas-powered data center planned by the DCIP Group, a technology infrastructure company, that could eventually cover around 1,300 acres, which would make it one of the largest in the world.

Ms. Gruters’s opponents in the primary were Eddie Speir, who founded a religious academy in Bradenton and opposes the data center project, and Ed Pope, a Navy veteran and former Florida Highway Patrol trooper who campaigned as a political outsider.

item.title: Democratic State Representative Scores Upset Win in Florida Senate Primary
item.description:
State Representative Angie Nixon of Jacksonville, a progressive firebrand who ran an underdog campaign, won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Florida, according to The Associated Press, the latest left-wing victory against establishment Democrats.

In a huge upset, Ms. Nixon, 42, defeated Alex Vindman, a former national security official who was a top witness in President Trump’s first impeachment trial. His entry was largely welcomed by Democratic Party leaders hoping to make Florida, which leans right, at least competitive this fall. Mr. Vindman far out-raised Ms. Nixon and was the clear front-runner in the race.

But there was no public polling ahead of the primary. Pollsters most likely saw little upside to spending money in a state that President Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024.

Ms. Nixon, a union organizer, ran a grass-roots campaign, often driving herself to events across the state — clad in her signature hot pink outfits — and relying on volunteers and union members for field organizing. In a low-turnout primary, they bet that reaching enough Democratic voters directly, and talking to them about issues such as unaffordable health care and child care, would drive them to the polls to support Ms. Nixon.

The strategy succeeded: Ms. Nixon defeated Mr. Vindman across Florida’s urban counties, including Miami-Dade and Broward, where Mr. Vindman has lived since he moved to the state in 2023.

“We came up short, but we have Angie Nixon,” Mr. Vindman told supporters inside an American Legion hall near Fort Lauderdale in his concession speech on Tuesday night. “Rep. Nixon ran a strong campaign. She challenged the status quo. She put in the hard work, and tonight, she earned the nomination.”

Ms. Nixon rolled to victory despite an enormous fund-raising disparity. She raised about $975,000 during the campaign, while Mr. Vindman, powered by a national donor network, raised $16.3 million. Mr. Vindman was so confident in winning Tuesday that he had a fund-raiser scheduled for Sunday in Nantucket, Mass., as he prepared for a costly general election.

That general election will now happen without him.

Ms. Nixon acknowledged the spending gap in her victory speech at her watch party in Jacksonville. “We have proved that everyday people are more powerful than corporations and billionaires,” she said, after being introduced by her mother.

“We were outspent 16 to 1, and we won,” she added. “This win was for the little guys and girls.”

Ms. Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, will now test whether a progressive can win over moderate Democrats, as well as independents and crossover Republicans, in an increasingly red state.

She will challenge Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, in November.

In Jacksonville, where Ms. Nixon held her watch party, a big crowd jumped as they watched the results on television. “This is what democracy looks like,” they chanted.

“She’s for the people,” said Kaydene Williams, who attended the party. “She makes herself available to the people.”

Although Ms. Moody is the sitting senator, Democrats see her as potentially vulnerable in a tough midterm year for Republicans. She has held the position only since last year, having been appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, after Marco Rubio left the post to become secretary of state. She remains little known among Florida voters, polls show, even after winning two terms as the state’s attorney general.

But Republicans have clear structural advantages in Florida elections, including more robust fund-raising and field organization. And Democrats have tended to bet on moderates to unseat Republican incumbents.

Ms. Nixon, who is the clear underdog to Ms. Moody in the Florida Senate race, said in a brief interview with The New York Times on Tuesday night that she would defy expectations in November the same way she had won the Democratic primary: “By going out and having conversations with people.”

“They are going to lie and call me all kinds of names,” she added. “If I want to profess to be the next U.S. senator, I have to meet people where they are and talk to them.”

Susan Cooper Eastman contributed reporting from Jacksonville, Fla.

item.title: David Jolly Wins Democratic Nomination for Florida Governor
item.description:
Former Representative David Jolly, a Republican turned Democrat and a strong critic of President Trump, won the Democratic nomination for Florida governor on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

Mr. Jolly, 53, will be the underdog in the general-election race to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican who has solidified the state as a conservative stronghold.

Mr. Jolly defeated the second-placed finisher, Dayna Marie Foster, a liberal former teacher from Fort Lauderdale who was endorsed by Florida’s Democratic Progressive Caucus. Placing third was State Representative Dotie Joseph of North Miami, who entered the race late to give Democrats a more progressive choice. An earlier contender, Mayor Jerry Demings of Orange County, home to Orlando, dropped out of the race before the qualifying deadline, citing a cancer diagnosis.

Mr. Jolly, a lawyer, served as a Republican congressman from 2014 to 2017. He left the Republican Party in 2018 and has been a frequent political commentator on cable news. He held no party affiliation until registering as a Democrat last year.

Although Florida was a hotly contested political battleground for years, registered Republicans in the state now handily outnumber Democrats. The party has not won a governor’s race since 1994, although Democrats came close eight years ago when Andrew Gillum, a Democrat, narrowly lost to Mr. DeSantis.

In an expensive state with multiple media markets, Representative Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor endorsed by Mr. Trump, has raised more than $100 million, far surpassing Mr. Jolly’s $10 million.

Still, Mr. Jolly has sought to tie Republicans to the broader voter discontent with Mr. Trump that helped Democrats win two special elections in Florida this year. Mr. Jolly has positioned himself as a moderate who will attack the state’s affordability crisis. And he is betting on voters to be fatigued by the culture battles waged by Mr. DeSantisAt a rally on Tuesday in Miami Lakes, Fla., Mr. Jolly urged voters in November to reject divisive rhetoric in favor of a government that is both lean and compassionate. “We are celebrating the return of a resiliency, the renewal of a hope, the belief in each other once again,” Mr. Jolly said.

He also cast Mr. Donalds as beholden to big-money corporate interests. “Everybody in this state can pull up a chair to the table. But money doesn’t buy access,” Mr. Jolly said.

item.title: Byron Donalds Wins Republican Nomination for Florida Governor
item.description:
Representative Byron Donalds, who was endorsed by President Trump, easily secured the Republican nomination for Florida governor on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

Mr. Donalds now faces the Democratic candidate David Jolly in the November midterm election. Mr. Donalds, 47, will be favored to win the general election in a state that Mr. Trump calls home and that has shifted toward Republicans during the past decade.

Rick Scott, now a senator.
